node-1.label: 50-year-old female presented with abdominal pain, nausea, and progressive fatigue starting a few weeks before hospitalization

node-2.label: Symptoms began a few weeks before hospitalization, following treatment with oral antibiotics for a dental infection

node-3.label: Medical history included smoldering myeloma (diagnosed weeks before admission), autoimmune thyroiditis (since 2018), and Sjogren's syndrome (since 2020)

node-4.label: Physical examination showed normal vitals, enlarged liver, and bilateral leg edema

why.why: Laboratory and radiology expert analyses describe a cholestatic enzyme pattern (elevated ALP, AST, GGT, and INR with normal ALT/bilirubin) typical of drug-induced liver injury, and negative viral serology with leukocytosis adds support. The temporal link with oral antibiotic treatment remains strong. Confidence is raised from 0.4 to 0.65, but missing antibiotic name/dose/duration and autoimmune serologies prevent higher certainty.

Laboratory analysis showing polyclonal gammopathy without a monoclonal component directly reduces concern for smoldering myeloma progression. The cholestatic liver injury pattern and clear antibiotic temporal link further favor drug-induced hepatotoxicity over spontaneous myeloma progression. Confidence is lowered from 0.35 to 0.15.

Autoimmune serologies remain unavailable, so an autoimmune hepatic flare cannot be completely excluded; however, the predominantly cholestatic enzyme pattern (normal ALT/bilirubin with elevated ALP/GGT) is more typical of drug-induced injury than autoimmune hepatitis, and no new autoimmune-specific evidence has emerged. Confidence is reduced from 0.25 to 0.2.

node-8.label: Laboratory tests show elevated ALP, AST, GGT, and INR with normal ALT and bilirubin (cholestatic pattern)

node-9.label: Viral hepatitis serology is negative and leukocytosis is present

node-10.label: Serum protein electrophoresis shows polyclonal gammopathy without a monoclonal component
